ต้นกำเนิดของวัดปทุมธาราหรือวัดหน้าเมืองย: The origins of Wat Pathum Thara, or Wat Na Mueang, are told in two ways. Takua Pa Municipality records an oral account that Thao, the daughter of Phraya Takua Pa (Muang), built the temple in 1757 (B.E. 2320). The ONEP old-town database, however, explains that after the original town was destroyed and abandoned during the Burmese wars, the revival at Ban Talat Yai under the reign of Rama III began with the construction of Wat Na Mueang, followed by the governor's residence nearby
ภาพใหญ่ของตะกั่วป่าคือเมืองท่าริมแม่น้ำแ: Takua Pa's larger story is that of a riverside port and tin-trading center. The town prospered through mining and maritime trade, while Chinese workers, especially Hokkien Chinese, settled here and connected its culture with the Malay Peninsula. The temple therefore likely served as the main religious site for the Talat Yai community and a landmark of the newly re-established town, but the sources found do not identify a confirmed builder or the temple's daily ritual role in that period
ในยุคการค้าทางน้ำ วัดอยู่ใกล้พื้นที่ที่ม: During the era of waterborne trade, the temple stood near routes for travel and goods transport. A community source identifies the boiler on the temple grounds as part of a steamboat jointly purchased by Phraya Senanuchit (Nuch Na Nakhon) in 1867 (B.E. 2410) to carry goods and suppress pirates, before the vessel deteriorated and sank in the Takua Pa River. This evidence reflects the trading network, but it is not evidence that the temple itself operated a mine

The temple remained a religious and community space. Its monks' quarters once served as the first classroom site of Ban Si Takua Pa Municipal School, before the school moved to its current location in 1956 (B.E. 2499). The municipality states that the southern vernacular ordination hall was registered as an ancient monument in 1935 (B.E. 2478), but this research has not checked the original notice

วัดเสนานุชรังสรรค์ หรือที่ชาวบ้านเรียกว่: Wat Senanuch Rangsan, locally called "Wat Mai Kamphaeng," arose while Phraya Senanuchit (Nuch Na Nakhon) was governor of Takua Pa. A source from the Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn Anthropology Centre says the temple was built after the city wall, administrative office, and governor's residence were completed, giving it significance both as a Buddhist offering and as a memorial to its builder
พื้นที่เดิมเป็นเนินดินเชิงเขาฉมมังคิรี พ: The original site was an earthen rise at the foot of Chom Mangkhiri Mountain. Phraya Senanuchit had the ground leveled, then built a roughly 2-meter-high brick-and-mortar wall with east and west gates, followed by an ordination hall in the center and preaching halls on both sides. The name "Wat Mai Kamphaeng" therefore reflects more than a new temple: it reflects a townscape taking shape alongside governing power and a community center
ในยุคที่ตะกั่วป่ายังเป็นเมืองท่าฝั่งอันด: When Takua Pa was still an Andaman port linked to maritime trade and the tin economy, the temple's ordination hall was used for the oath of allegiance ceremony. This shows the temple directly linking religious ritual with the town's political order. The hall's Chinese-influenced design also fits Takua Pa's market district and Hokkien Chinese community, but the sources do not confirm that its craftsmen or patrons were directly Chinese
สำนักงานนโยบายและแผนทรัพยากรธรรมชาติและส: Office of Natural Resources and Environmental Policy and Planning (ONEP)
วัดยังเป็นสถานที่ประกอบพิธีถือน้ำพิพัฒน์: The temple continued to host the oath of allegiance ceremony before the 1932 (B.E. 2475) political change. Its history also records Phra Khru Udom Panya (Nuam) as abbot from 1865·1909 (B.E. 2408·2452), after which his students and followers built a stupa containing his ashes around 2014 (B.E. 2557). The temple thus holds layers of memory belonging both to the town and to the local monastic community
อาคารไม่ได้คงรูปเดิมทั้งหมด สารานุกรมวัฒ: The buildings have not retained their original form completely. The Thai Cultural Encyclopedia states that the ordination hall once had a three-tiered roof covered with scale tiles, but repairs reduced it to one tier and changed the roofing to corrugated metal. Another temple-register record says the current preaching hall was built in 1963 (B.E. 2506) and gives the date of its royal grant of Wisung Kham Sima as 8 January 1897 (B.E. 2440). However, some years in secondary sources contain printing or scanning errors, so they are not used as evidence for any additional restoration dates
กรมศิลปากรขึ้นทะเบียนโบราณสถานของวัดใน พ: The Fine Arts Department registered the temple as an ancient monument in 1996 (B.E. 2539), with its surrounding wall and large Chinese-influenced ordination hall as key features. Later, as part of the revival of Takua Pa old town, the temple also became home to the Takua Pa Community Museum, which collects tools and equipment from the mining way of life. The grounds therefore serve both as a religious site and as a place where the town's post-mining memories are told
